target.title: LTA-L2S: Lexical Tone-Aware Lip-to-Speech Synthesis for Mandarin with Cross-Lingual Transfer Learning

read.pdf: Fig. 1 and Tables 1-4 read from the text extraction; references [1]-[35] read

entries.text: The authors present LTA-L2S as a novel Mandarin lip-to-speech framework with two primary contributions.
entries.condition: Framework evaluated on the CN-CVS speech subset.

entries.text: The first contribution transfers an English-pretrained audio-visual encoder to Mandarin to address viseme-to-phoneme ambiguity and reduce the cost of training SSL from scratch.
entries.condition: AV-HuBERT Base initialized from English audio-visual pretraining, then fine-tuned on the Mandarin dataset.
entries.quote:
This approach effectively leverages
knowledge from English audio-visual data while reducing compu-
tational cost.

entries.text: The second contribution uses ASR-fine-tuned SSL speech units to guide flow-matching F0 generation for lexical tone modeling and intelligibility.
entries.condition: Mandarin L2S; target units are derived from layer-9 w2v2-ft features.
entries.quote:
This generation process
is guided by ASR-fine-tuned SSL speech units, which contain cru-
cial suprasegmental information.

entries.text: A flow-matching postnet refines the first-stage coarse spectrogram; the authors claim this raises overall speech quality.
entries.condition: Two-stage training; first-stage network frozen while the postnet is trained.
entries.quote:
The overall speech quality is
then elevated through a two-stage training paradigm, where a flow-
matching postnet refines the coarse spectrogram from the first stage.

entries.text: The authors claim significant superiority over existing methods in speech intelligibility and tonal accuracy.
entries.condition: Experiments on CN-CVS; objective CER and TER plus subjective intelligibility ratings.
entries.quote:
Extensive experiments demonstrate that LTA-L2S significantly out-
performs existing methods in both speech intelligibility and tonal
accuracy.

entries.text: The CN-CVS speech subset contains 273.4 hours of audio-visual data from 2,529 speakers.
entries.condition: CN-CVS speech subset; dataset-wide totals, not test-split totals.

entries.text: The authors use the original CN-CVS unseen-speaker split and exclude non-Mandarin sentences.
entries.condition: Official CN-CVS split; exact split counts and FunASR checkpoint are not specified.

entries.text: The visual encoder starts from AV-HuBERT Base weights pretrained on 1,759 hours of English data and is fine-tuned on Mandarin in stage one.
entries.unit: hours of English audio-visual pretraining data
entries.condition: AV-HuBERT Base visual encoder initialization; fine-tuned on the CN-CVS Mandarin training data.
entries.quote: we initialize this encoder with weights pre-trained on 1759 hours of English data and subsequently fine-tune it on our Mandarin dataset during the first training stage.

entries.text: The visual encoder architecture is AV-HuBERT Base.
entries.condition: Visual encoder of LTA-L2S.

entries.text: Target speech units come from k-means over layer-9 features of ASR-fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0.
entries.condition: ASR-fine-tuned w2v2-ft features; units used as unit-predictor training targets.
entries.quote: we extract the target units by applying k-means clustering to the 9th-layer features of an ASR-fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 model (w2v2-ft) [19, 20].

entries.text: The speech-unit inventory has 2,000 k-means clusters.
entries.condition: Unit labels from layer-9 w2v2-ft features; predictor trained against those labels.
entries.quote:
The discrete speech units are derived by using k-
means algorithm with 2000 clusters.

entries.text: The unit predictor has four Conformer blocks and a final linear layer.
entries.condition: First-stage unit prediction from visual features.

entries.text: YAAPT extracts pitch targets from raw audio, which are separated into continuous F0 contours and discrete voiced/unvoiced labels.
entries.condition: Training supervision for the pitch predictor; no F0 scale normalization is stated.
entries.quote:
We employ the YAAPT algorithm [22] to extract the pitch
sequence from raw audio, which is then decomposed into a contin-
uous F0 contour and discrete UV labels.

entries.text: At inference, F0 is generated from Gaussian noise by solving an ODE from t=0 to t=1 with Euler updates.
entries.condition: Flow-matching condition combines upsampled visual, unit, and speaker embeddings.
entries.quote: the final F0 counter is generated by sampling an initial point x0 ∼ N(0, I)

entries.text: The pitch predictor conditions on a speaker embedding extracted from a pretrained speaker-verification model; the paper does not identify the reference audio source or enrollment protocol.
entries.condition: Speaker embedding is an additional model condition besides video; evaluation protocol for supplying it is unspecified.
entries.quote:
Consis-
tent with prior works [8, 24], the speaker embeddings are extracted
from a pre-trained speaker verification model2.

entries.text: The mel decoder follows FastSpeech 2 with six FFT blocks and reconstructs mel spectrograms using visual, unit, speaker, and pitch embeddings.
entries.condition: Stage-one coarse mel-spectrogram generation.

entries.text: Stage one weights unit, UV, F0, and mel losses by 0.1, 1.0, 1.0, and 1.0, respectively.
entries.unit: loss weights λunit, λuv, λf0, λmel
entries.condition: Two training stages; stage-one objective is the weighted sum of component losses.

entries.text: Visual preprocessing crops aligned frames to 96×96 grayscale patches centered on the lips.
entries.condition: CN-CVS input preprocessing; image-intensity normalization is not specified.

entries.text: Training runs 100 epochs per stage on two NVIDIA 4090 GPUs at batch size 16 per GPU.
entries.condition: Both training stages; random seeds, validation use, and checkpoint selection are not reported.

entries.text: Both F0 and postnet inference use Sway sampling with 24 function evaluations.
entries.unit: NFE for each of F0 predictor and postnet
entries.condition: Inference decoding; Euler ODE solver specified for F0, postnet uses an ODE solver.

entries.text: The system refines a coarse mel spectrogram to a fine-grained mel spectrogram, then uses HiFi-GAN to produce the waveform.
entries.condition: HiFi-GAN vocoder pretrained on CN-CVS speech data.

entries.text: CER and TER are computed from FunASR transcripts post-processed by g2pM.
entries.condition: CN-CVS evaluation; model/checkpoint and decoding configuration of FunASR are not specified.
entries.quote:
Both are computed from FunASR transcrip-
tions post-processed by the g2pM library4.

entries.text: The MOS protocol used 15 native Mandarin listeners, 30 samples per model, and a 5-point scale for naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity.
entries.unit: listeners; samples per model; rating-scale points
entries.condition: Subjective CN-CVS evaluation; assignment, randomization, blinding, repeats, and meaning of reported ± are unstated.
entries.quote: 15 native Mandarin speakers rated 30 samples per model on a 5-point scale for naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity.

entries.text: The authors claim state-of-the-art intelligibility, with the lowest CER and TER among compared systems.
entries.condition: CN-CVS objective evaluation; official unseen-speaker split; FunASR transcripts post-processed with g2pM; LTA-L2S uses Sway/NFE 24 and HiFi-GAN; baseline decode settings are not fully detailed.

entries.text: The authors say speech quality scores rank second only to LTBS on STOI-Net and DNSMOS.
entries.condition: CN-CVS objective evaluation; Table 1 comparator rows; exact baseline-specific decoding settings are not given.

entries.text: The authors claim the highest speaker similarity, reporting SECS 0.828.
entries.condition: CN-CVS objective evaluation; embeddings from Resemblyzer.

entries.text: The authors report that LTA-L2S is preferred over every baseline on all three subjective dimensions.
entries.condition: MOS listening test; 15 native Mandarin speakers and 30 samples per model; ± statistic not defined.

entries.text: The authors attribute LTBS's lower subjective naturalness to its poorer intelligibility despite its high objective quality scores.
entries.condition: Interpretation of objective and subjective results; no causal test is reported.

entries.text: Removing the postnet lowers DNSMOS; the authors interpret this as evidence that it improves naturalness and fine acoustic detail.
entries.condition: Ablation on CN-CVS; Table 3; other training settings and run variability are not stated.

entries.text: Replacing flow-matching F0 with simple L1 optimization raises CER and TER; the authors claim this supports their flow-matching approach.
entries.condition: Ablation labeled w/o f0 cfm on CN-CVS; Table 3.

entries.text: The authors say removing the full pitch predictor reduces STOI-Net and DNSMOS.
entries.condition: Ablations on CN-CVS; Table 3.

entries.text: The authors report that random visual-encoder initialization raises CER and TER.
entries.condition: Cross-lingual and unit-source ablations on CN-CVS; Table 4.

entries.text: The authors attribute the w2v2-ft unit ablation's error increase to losing both semantic supervision and supplementary lexical-tone information.
entries.condition: Compared with layer-9, 2,000-cluster HuBERT units on CN-CVS; Table 4.

entries.text: The authors place extension to other Chinese dialects and accents in future work; these are outside the reported evaluation scope.
entries.condition: Reported experiments are on the CN-CVS Mandarin speech subset.

entries.text: Exact test-split composition is absent: no held-out utterance count, speaker count, duration, or session count is reported.
entries.condition: Only the original CN-CVS unseen-speaker split and dataset-wide size are stated.

entries.condition: Training is described as 100 epochs per stage; use of validation data is not stated.

entries.condition: Applies to main results and ablations; MOS reports ± but its statistic is undefined.
entries.quote: The model is optimized using AdamW [29] with a learning rate that peaks at 1e-4

entries.text: Although the split is called unseen-speaker, train/test speaker counts and an explicit speaker-overlap audit are not reported.
entries.condition: CN-CVS original split; no split-level participant or session breakdown.

entries.text: The paper does not define an output character vocabulary or report an external LM; the generator predicts discrete speech units and produces audio.
entries.condition: The unit inventory is specified as 2,000 clusters; language-model use in synthesis is not stated.

entries.text: The FunASR model/checkpoint, version, language-model or beam settings, and decoding options used to create CER/TER transcripts are not named.
entries.condition: CER/TER calculated from FunASR transcripts then post-processed with g2pM.

entries.text: Transcript normalization details for CER/TER (punctuation, numerals, script variants, and manual verification) are not specified; no F0 scaling or image-intensity normalization is stated either.
entries.condition: Data preprocessing reports grayscale crops and mel extraction; the metric pipeline names FunASR and g2pM only.

entries.text: No chance-level, random, or majority baseline is reported for CER, TER, or the MOS ratings.
entries.condition: Comparisons include named L2S baselines and ground-truth audio, but no chance-level reference.

entries.text: The MOS study does not say whether every listener rated every sample, how clips were randomized or blinded, whether ratings were repeated, or whether ± is SD, SE, or another interval.

entries.quote: 15 native Mandarin speakers rated 30 samples per model on a 5-point scale

entries.text: The model architecture includes speaker embeddings, but the paper does not say how a test speaker's embedding is obtained in the unseen-speaker, lips-only setup.
entries.condition: Speaker embedding comes from a pretrained speaker-verification model; reference-audio access, duration, and enrollment policy are unspecified.
entries.quote: The process begins with a visual encoder and a unit pre- dictor that predict speech units from the silent lip video.

entries.text: The paper does not state how the YAAPT F0 targets are scaled or normalized before training the flow-matching predictor.
entries.condition: YAAPT pitch sequence separated into continuous F0 and discrete UV labels; normalization details absent.

entries.text: The linked g2pM source defaults to tone=True and char_split=False; the paper does not report call flags or a pinned repository revision for CER/TER post-processing.
entries.condition: Code-only default in the linked g2pM repository; the paper only says transcripts are post-processed with g2pM.

entries.text: The linked Real-Time-Voice-Cloning embed_utterance defaults to 160-frame partials, 50% overlap, 75% minimum final-partial coverage, and an L2-normalized mean of partial embeddings; the paper does not specify extraction settings.
entries.unit: partial length; overlap; minimum coverage; aggregation
entries.condition: Condition in the linked repository's current unpinned branch, not a pinned LTA-L2S implementation; applied only if that embedding path is used.

entries.text: The linked speaker-encoder preprocessing defaults to volume normalization toward -30 dBFS (increase-only) and silence trimming when WebRTC VAD is available; paper-level speaker-audio preprocessing is not stated.
entries.condition: normalize=True and trim_silence=True defaults in linked code; VAD trimming is conditional on successful WebRTC VAD import.

entries.text: The F0 and postnet DiT backbones use 8 attention heads, 512-dimensional embeddings, and a 1,024-dimensional feed-forward network.
entries.unit: attention heads; embedding dimensions; feed-forward dimensions
entries.condition: Architectural settings for F0 predictor and postnet.

entries.text: The Table 4 transfer-ablation paragraph says CER and PER, while Table 4 labels the corresponding metric TER; the paper does not resolve this prose/table mismatch.
entries.value: PER in prose; TER in table

entries.quote: increase in both CER and PER

entries.condition: Prediction targets are the 2,000 k-means clusters from layer-9 ASR-fine-tuned w2v2 features.

entries.text: The visual encoder alignment step extracts 68 facial landmarks per frame using dlib.
entries.condition: Visual preprocessing before crop extraction.

entries.text: Audio input is sampled at 16 kHz and represented with 80 mel filters, a 40 ms analysis window, and 10 ms hop.
entries.unit: Hz; mel filters; ms window; ms hop

entries.text: Visual encoder frames are temporally upsampled by a factor of two to match the speech-unit frame rate.
entries.condition: Transposed 1D convolution before the unit predictor.

entries.text: The training schedule uses AdamW with peak learning rate 1e-4, 10-epoch linear warm-up, then cosine decay.
entries.condition: Both training stages; random seeds and validation/checkpoint selection are not specified.

entries.text: Teacher forcing is used throughout training.
entries.condition: Training protocol; scope described as throughout.

entries.text: The authors motivate flow matching as a way to model complex F0 contour variation.
entries.condition: F0 predictor for Mandarin lexical tone synthesis.

We employ a Diffu-
sion Transformer (DiT) [25] as the estimator’s backbone and opti-
mize it using the Rectified Flow Matching (RFM) [26] loss:

entries.text: The test-set reference text labels are re-transcribed using a FunASR model.

entries.quote: we re-transcribed the text labels for the test set using FunASR model3.

entries.text: The authors say layer 9 of the ASR-fine-tuned SSL model has the strongest tone-classification performance and thus richer suprasegmental information.
entries.condition: Layer selection rationale for speech-unit targets.

entries.text: The authors say the postnet refines fine-grained acoustic detail and counters over-smoothing caused by L1 spectrogram loss.
entries.condition: Second training stage, conditioned on coarse spectrogram and mel-decoder input.

entries.text: The authors report substantial performance degradation when speech-unit supervision is removed.
entries.condition: CN-CVS ablation; Table 3.

entries.text: Replacing w2v2-ft speech units with HuBERT units increases CER and TER, according to the authors.
entries.condition: HuBERT comparison uses k=2000 clusters on layer-9 features; CN-CVS ablation.

entries.text: Objective metrics include DNSMOS and STOI-Net for speech quality, and Resemblyzer embeddings for SECS speaker similarity.
entries.condition: Objective evaluation on CN-CVS.

entries.text: F0 DiT depth is 8 layers and postnet DiT depth is 12 layers.
entries.condition: Different depths for the F0 predictor and postnet DiT backbones.

entries.text: Generated mel-spectrograms from the successive generator resolutions are projected through 1×1 convolutions and sent to multi-discriminators.
entries.condition: Multi-scale outputs; one discriminator loss per scale

entries.text: GAN training combines unconditional mel-spectrogram realism and conditional agreement with temporally averaged global visual context; generated mel-spectrograms also receive L1 reconstruction supervision.
entries.condition: Conditional context is M(Cv), temporal average pooling of global visual features

entries.text: The coarse generator concatenates standard-normal noise with repeated visual features; no explicit pitch or energy predictor or control is described.
entries.condition: Noise seed and sampling procedure are not reported

entries.text: For waveform output, a postnet maps generated mel-spectrograms to linear spectrograms and Griffin-Lim reconstructs the waveform; the postnet uses L1 reconstruction loss.
entries.condition: Listening/waveform evaluation path

entries.text: Evaluation covers GRID (constrained speakers 1, 2, 4, 29; unseen-speaker split 15/8/10 train/validation/test; multi-speaker all 33 with the VSR protocol), TCD-TIMIT (3 lip speakers for constrained evaluation), and LRW (500 words, up to 1,000 training videos per word).
entries.condition: GRID split details and benchmark-specific settings as stated

entries.text: Objective measures are STOI and ESTOI for intelligibility (higher is better), PESQ for perceptual quality (higher is better), and WER for recognized content (lower is better). WER uses ASR trained for each setting; provider/model differences make some cross-method WER comparisons non-equivalent.
entries.condition: WER uses ASR; GRID constrained comparison uses Google ASR, while other reported WERs include setting-trained ASR

entries.text: MOS study: 12 participants rated intelligibility, naturalness, and synchronization on a 1–5 scale, using 20 samples per method from constrained-speaker GRID.
entries.condition: Constrained-speaker GRID; four methods plus ground truth; 20 samples per method

entries.text: GRID has 1,000 unique sentences, a 51-word vocabulary, and 33 speakers; the seen split includes the same speakers across train/validation/test, while the unseen split has no speaker overlap.

entries.text: LRS3 contains 312 hours, more than 50,000 words, and thousands of speakers; its seen protocol uses an utterance-level 80/10/10 train/validation/test split, and unseen follows the original split.

entries.text: The prior uses RAVEn to pretrain audio-visual representations on unlabeled multilingual AVSpeech (about 4,700 hours; languages include English, Portuguese, Spanish, French, Italian, and Mandarin), then transfers the visual encoder to visual speech recognition.
entries.condition: AVSpeech pretraining is self-supervised and uses unlabeled audio-video.

entries.text: Transfer direction is multilingual AVSpeech encoder pretraining → visual-only encoder initialized from pretraining → separate labeled visual-speech-recognition fine-tuning per target language.
entries.condition: Fine-tuning data: LRS3 English 30 h; TEDx Spanish 62 h, French 72 h, Portuguese 73 h, Italian 40 h; CMLR Mandarin 60.5 h. Mandarin uses characters; other languages use 1,000 subword units. A linear layer and Transformer decoder use joint CTC/attention loss, beam size 40, CTC weight 0.1. External-LM use, seeds, and speaker counts are not reported.

entries.text: The six-language Multilingual model reports 15.8% CER for Mandarin (zh) in Table 1.
entries.condition: Table 1 orders language columns en, it, pt, fr, es, zh. CMLR has 60.5 h train, 8.5 h validation, and 17 h test; Table 1 does not explicitly identify the scored split. Mandarin character targets; CTC/attention, beam size 40, CTC weight 0.1. External-LM use, seeds, and speaker counts are not reported.

entries.text: The Mandarin Monolingual model reports 22.6% CER, compared with 15.8% for six-language Multilingual pretraining under the Table 1 setup.
entries.condition: Fine-tuning is on CMLR Mandarin (60.5 h); the evaluated partition is not explicitly identified in Table 1. Mandarin character targets; CTC/attention, beam size 40, CTC weight 0.1. External-LM use, seeds, and speaker counts are not reported.

entries.text: CMLR is split into 60.5 h training, 8.5 h validation, and 17 h test; although Table 1 reports CER, it does not specify which split was scored.
entries.condition: Do not treat the dataset's named test split as explicitly confirmed for the Table 1 CER.

entries.text: These are visual speech recognition/transcription CER results, not evidence of speech waveform synthesis; the paper reports no generated waveform or synthesis-quality evaluation.
entries.condition: The reported task evaluates recognized text; no waveform synthesis metrics are presented.

entries.text: Speech units are derived by quantizing HuBERT-BASE self-supervised speech representations with K-means; the codebook is trained on LJ Speech, has 200 clusters, and outputs units at 50 Hz.
entries.condition: The units are extracted from paired speech audio and used as frame-level content targets; 20 ms mel frames are stacked to match the 50 Hz unit rate.

entries.text: A ResNet-18 visual front end and Conformer encode the lip video; a speaker-specific 1D-CNN predictor outputs mel-spectrogram conditioned on a d-vector speaker embedding, while a speaker-agnostic MLP predicts units. Training uses L1 mel reconstruction plus unit cross-entropy; no stochastic or search-based decoder is described.
entries.value: Mel: speaker-specific predictor; units: speaker-agnostic predictor
entries.condition: The speaker d-vector is extracted from a speech segment using a pretrained speaker-verification model.

entries.text: Waveform generation uses a GAN-based HiFi-GAN modification conditioned on mel-spectrogram, speech units, and speaker embedding. Unit embeddings (128-D) are upsampled to the mel rate and concatenated with mel; the speaker embedding is projected to 128-D and repeated. Vocoder training adds blur and Gaussian noise to mel inputs.
entries.condition: The vocoder is trained separately for each dataset; mel augmentation simulates blurry and noisy predicted spectrograms.

entries.text: On LRS3, the standard proposed system reports STOI 0.543, ESTOI 0.351, PESQ 1.28, and WER 50.2%; the A V-HuBERT variant reports 0.578, 0.393, 1.31, and 29.8%, respectively.
entries.condition: LRS3 test set; split follows [8] for unseen-speaker testing. The standard proposed row uses the paper's ResNet-18 front end; A V-HuBERT is a separate visual-front-end variant.

entries.text: On LRS2, the standard proposed system reports STOI 0.565, ESTOI 0.395, PESQ 1.32, and WER 44.8%; the A V-HuBERT variant reports 0.585, 0.412, 1.34, and 35.7%, respectively.
entries.condition: LRS2 test set; the dataset has thousands of speakers but provides no speaker information. A V-HuBERT is a separate visual-front-end variant.

entries.text: Human MOS for the proposed model on LRS3 is 4.40 naturalness, 3.92 intelligibility, and 4.15 clearness (reported uncertainty: ±0.13, ±0.15, and ±0.15).
entries.condition: 15 participants rated 20 randomly selected LRS3 test samples on a 1 (least) to 5 (most) scale; human evaluation uses the same visual encoder as prior work, not A V-HuBERT.

entries.text: Objective metrics are computed on each dataset's test set. LRS3 follows [8] for unseen-speaker testing; LRS2 has no speaker metadata. WER is obtained by recognizing generated speech with a pretrained model trained on audio from the corresponding dataset. The paper does not report vocabulary constraints, a decoding/search or language-model policy, or random seeds.

questions.q: What exact held-out speaker and test-set composition supports the reported generalization result?
questions.answer: The paper names the original CN-CVS unseen-speaker split and excludes non-Mandarin sentences, but gives no split-level utterance, speaker, duration, or session counts and no explicit overlap audit.

questions.q: How reproducible are the CER and TER comparisons, including ASR and text normalization?
questions.answer: The paper identifies FunASR and g2pM but omits the ASR checkpoint/version, decoding configuration, text-normalization rules, call flags, random seeds, and repeated-run variability; the linked g2pM default is tone=True and char_split=False.

questions.q: Does inference require reference audio in addition to silent lip video to obtain a speaker embedding?
questions.answer: A pretrained speaker-verification embedding is part of the architecture, but the paper does not specify its source or enrollment protocol; the linked helper code describes one possible extraction path, not a pinned LTA-L2S implementation.
